subject: Replay
claim: Canon is a reasoning engine: it decides from declared rules, refuses what it can't justify, and keeps a signed record of every decision that can be replayed.
FACT: Canon decides from declared rules, refuses decisions it can't justify from them, and writes a signed record of each decision that can be replayed.
COUNTER: Refusing what it can't justify makes Canon only as capable as its rule set; a gap in the rules looks the same as a correct refusal.
OPINION: Refusal over invention is the right default for a system meant to be trusted.
FICTION: Suppose a rule is missing for a common case; Canon refuses it every time, and the refusal log becomes the to-do list of rules to write.
CONTEXT: JIG is Canon's deterministic rule-engine substrate; LLLM is its language layer.

subject: Replay
claim: In Canon the LLM is only a surface: nothing authorises itself, and audit is replay.
FACT: In Canon the LLM only shapes wording; it never authorises an action or decides what is true, and audit is done by replaying the record.
COUNTER: If the LLM rephrases an answer, the wording people read isn't the exact thing that was decided, so the surface can still mislead.
OPINION: Keeping the model at the surface is what makes Canon auditable at all.
FICTION: Suppose the LLM is swapped for another model; every decision replays identically, and only the phrasing changes.
CONTEXT: Same principle as Keystone Gate: the LLM handles language, never truth arbitration.

claim: Canon's phases 0 to 40 are largely built.
FACT: James states Canon's phases 0 to 40 are largely built.
COUNTER: 'Largely' isn't measurable; the cube can't be checked until it says which phases are done and how 'done' is judged.
OPINION: Worth replacing with a per-phase status list, the way Replicant's README has a status table.
FICTION: Suppose phase 23 is half-built; 'largely built' hides it until someone depends on it.
CONTEXT: Phase 0 is documentation. Needs a source: a CHANGELOG or a phase list.

subject: Determinism
claim: Canon is built and tested on a phone in Termux, with no cloud, no vendor and no model in the loop.
FACT: Canon is built and tested on a phone in Termux, with no cloud service, no vendor and no model in its decision loop.
COUNTER: kg ask --claude adds an optional cloud model beside SymLM for phrasing, so 'no model' holds for decisions, not for every output.
OPINION: Running on a phone is the strongest proof of sovereignty the project has.
FICTION: Suppose the network drops for a week; every Canon decision still runs and replays.
CONTEXT: Tools stay on Python's standard library, the only optional third-party package being the Anthropic SDK.

subject: ChronoSCRIBE
claim: ChronoSCRIBE keeps the authoritative ledger: time-ordered, hash-chained and signed, holding every document and capsule hash and every HAL seal.
FACT: ChronoSCRIBE keeps the authoritative ledger: time-ordered, hash-chained and signed entries for every document hash, capsule hash and HAL seal.
COUNTER: With one operator key signing everything, the ledger proves order and integrity, not independent witnessing.
OPINION: The ledger is what turns the other stages from claims into history.
FICTION: Suppose a capsule is edited after signing; its hash no longer matches its ledger entry, and verification fails at that row.
CONTEXT: Ledger rows pin scp_id plus sha256, not file paths. Published rows are never discarded.

subject: ChronoSCRIBE
claim: Without ChronoSCRIBE, decay values and trust scores are assertions; with it, they are verifiable history.
FACT: The stack's own docs say that without ChronoSCRIBE, decay values and trust scores are assertions, and with it they become verifiable history.
COUNTER: A ledger only proves what was written to it; a score computed from unlogged events is still an assertion.
OPINION: This is the clearest one-line reason the Audit stage exists.
FICTION: Suppose λ is reported but its events were never logged; nobody can replay how the number was reached.
CONTEXT: ChronoSCRIBE must stay fully compiled, with no capsule-declared content.

subject: DataCube
claim: DataCube grades a cube's completeness: CRYSTALLINE at 90% or more, COHERENT 70–89%, FORMING 40–69% and SPARSE under 40%.
FACT: DataCube grades completeness: CRYSTALLINE at 90% or more, COHERENT 70–89%, FORMING 40–69%, SPARSE below 40%.
COUNTER: Completeness counts filled faces, not good ones; a cube full of weak AI drafts can still grade CRYSTALLINE.
OPINION: Useful as a triage signal, but it should never stand in for human validation.
FICTION: Suppose every face is accepted unread; the grade reads CRYSTALLINE while nothing was checked.
CONTEXT: The SCP substrate doesn't implement these grades yet.

subject: DataCube
claim: DataCube keeps an append-only store, never called a ledger, because that word belongs to ChronoSCRIBE.
FACT: DataCube keeps an append-only store, and the stack's terminology reserves the word 'ledger' for ChronoSCRIBE.
COUNTER: Append-only but unchained and unsigned, the store can't prove it wasn't rewritten.
OPINION: Keeping the words separate stops people assuming the store has ledger guarantees.
FICTION: Suppose a doc calls the store a ledger; a reader assumes it's hash-chained, and it isn't.
CONTEXT: Ratified terminology: DataCube is the system, cube the artefact, store the container.

subject: DataCube
claim: DataCube classifies through six lenses, FACT, COUNTER, OPINION, FICTION, CONTEXT and UNKNOWN, and a cube is complete only when all six are filled.
FACT: The Forge Stack glossary defines six lenses, FACT, COUNTER, OPINION, FICTION, CONTEXT and UNKNOWN, and calls a cube complete only when all six are filled.
COUNTER: This conflicts with later decisions: Day 1 of the-forge corrected DataCube to five lenses plus a contradicts field, James later said DataCube is variable, Replicant drops FICTION, and the SCP substrate drops UNKNOWN.
OPINION: The glossary should be updated to say lens sets are per-consumer, or this cube will keep contradicting its neighbours.
FICTION: Suppose a consumer is audited against the six-lens rule; Replicant and the SCP substrate both fail it, by design.
CONTEXT: Conflicts with scp-substrate-has-five-lenses and Replicant's five-lens set.

subject: DataCube
claim: An empty COUNTER lens signals that disconfirming evidence hasn't been sought.
FACT: An empty COUNTER lens means disconfirming evidence hasn't been sought, not that none exists.
COUNTER: A cube can also have an empty COUNTER because the claim is trivially true; the signal needs judgement, not automation.
OPINION: One of the most useful rules in the stack.
FICTION: Suppose a swarm never checks claims; its COUNTER bin stays empty and it looks confident right up until a poisoned trail starves it.
CONTEXT: Replicant uses the same diagnostic for its swarm.

subject: SCP
claim: Every sc must be signed, SCP Lite capsules included.
FACT: Every sc must carry an Ed25519 signature, including SCP Lite capsules.
COUNTER: The SCP substrate doesn't sign the capsules or cubes it creates itself, so the rule isn't enforced everywhere yet.
OPINION: Signing is cheap and deterministic, so there's little reason for exceptions.
FICTION: Suppose an unsigned capsule slips into sc/; sign.py's guards are what should refuse it.
CONTEXT: Signed means provenance, not trust.

claim: AXIOM and Mimir are no longer part of the Forge Stack spine.
FACT: AXIOM and Mimir are out of scope for the Forge Stack spine: tools built with the stack, not part of it.
COUNTER: 'Retired' and 'out of scope' aren't the same; Mimir still exists as an sc-bound LLM, and AXIOM has a gravestone doc.
OPINION: Say 'out of scope', not 'retired', to match the AXIOM gravestone wording.
FICTION: Suppose someone reads 'retired' and deletes Mimir's binding capsule.
CONTEXT: AXIOM's 'incapable of hallucination' claim was formally withdrawn for a traceability framing.

claim: The Forge Stack is a five-stage spine: Declare (SCP), Classify (DataCube), Trust-score (Leighton Weight), Audit (ChronoSCRIBE) and Act (HAL).
FACT: The Forge Stack's spine has five stages: Declare (SCP), Classify (DataCube), Trust-score (Leighton Weight), Audit (ChronoSCRIBE) and Act (HAL).
COUNTER: A sixth stage, Decide (RuleEngine), was later added, and each stage is now adopted independently per consumer rather than walked as a fixed pipeline.
OPINION: Update the claim to six stages, optional per consumer, or mark it as describing v1.
FICTION: Suppose a new consumer builds all five stages because the cube says so, when it only needed Declare.
CONTEXT: RuleEngine still needs its own governance capsule.

claim: The Forge Stack is enforced at runtime by the gate pattern: ingress gates protect state, and egress gates protect the world.
FACT: The Forge Stack is enforced at runtime by gates: ingress gates protect internal state, and egress gates protect the outside world.
COUNTER: A gate is only as strong as its rules; a permissive gate enforces nothing.
OPINION: Naming both directions is the useful part: most systems only guard input.
FICTION: Suppose an egress gate is skipped for speed; a quarantined agent can still act on the world.
CONTEXT: Keystone Gate is the clearest example of the pattern.

claim: Each Forge Stack stage pairs a named system with a lowercase artefact: SCP makes an sc, DataCube a cube, ChronoSCRIBE a ledger and HAL a seal, while Leighton Weight's output is the number λ.
FACT: Each stage pairs a named system with a lowercase artefact: SCP makes an sc, DataCube a cube, ChronoSCRIBE a ledger, HAL a seal, and Leighton Weight outputs the number λ.
COUNTER: λ isn't an artefact in the same sense; it's computed on the fly and never stored, so the pairing breaks at that stage.
OPINION: The naming discipline makes docs and code far easier to read.
FICTION: Suppose code names a variable 'capsule'; the rule says sc in schemas and code, capsule only in prose.
CONTEXT: Ratified terminology, British English throughout.

claim: Forge Stack terms are defined once, in its glossary, and a change to the glossary makes a new capsule identity rather than an edit.
FACT: Forge Stack terms are defined once, in its glossary, and changing the glossary creates a new capsule identity rather than an edit.
COUNTER: A single source only helps if every doc defers to it; the six-lens definition shows the glossary can fall behind decisions.
OPINION: Versioned definitions are right: old capsules keep the meaning they were signed under.
FICTION: Suppose a term is quietly redefined; every old capsule's meaning shifts, which this rule prevents.
CONTEXT: Matches the rule that inherits records the governance in force at signing.

claim: Forge Stack v1 is frozen, signed and witnessed: eleven capsules signed with James's own did:key, and nineteen genesis entries in the ledger.
FACT: Forge Stack v1 is frozen, signed and witnessed: eleven capsules signed with James's did:key and nineteen genesis entries in the ledger.
COUNTER: Signed and witnessed by the same single operator; frozen proves it hasn't changed, not that anyone else reviewed it.
OPINION: A frozen, signed baseline is what later versions can be measured against.
FICTION: Suppose a v1 capsule is edited; re-signing produces a different signature and the freeze check fails.
CONTEXT: Ed25519 is deterministic, so re-signing unchanged content gives byte-identical signatures.

subject: Leighton Weight
claim: Forge Theory's decay formula N(t) = N₀·e^(−kt) belongs to the whole stack, and its decay constant k is calibrated per domain and doesn't transfer between domains.
FACT: Forge Theory's decay formula N(t) = N₀·e^(−kt) belongs to the whole stack, and k is calibrated per domain and doesn't transfer.
COUNTER: The stack's ratified λ decay pulls toward neutral 1.00, λ(t) = 1.00 + (λ₀ − 1.00)·e^(−kt), not toward zero, so the bare formula isn't how trust decays.
OPINION: Per-domain k is the important half; a constant tuned for pheromones means nothing for reputation.
FICTION: Suppose a k calibrated for Replicant claims is reused for HAL authorisers; trust fades at an insect's pace.
CONTEXT: --k-per-day is mandatory in leighton_weight.py to enforce per-domain calibration.

subject: HAL
claim: HAL has five tiers of authorisation mapped to λ, from Tier 1 (0.60–0.89, easily reversible actions) to Tier 5 (1.80–2.00, root council).
FACT: HAL has five authorisation tiers mapped to λ, from Tier 1 (0.60–0.89, easily reversible actions) to Tier 5 (1.80–2.00, root council).
COUNTER: With one operator key, no one can currently hold independent Tier 5 authority; the tiers record intent.
OPINION: Tying tier to reversibility is the right axis.
FICTION: Suppose λ drifts below a tier boundary mid-task; HAL refuses the next seal, even for the same operator.
CONTEXT: Tier-to-consequence mapping is consumer-defined; the stack provides the ladder. Tier 0 needs no λ.

subject: HAL
claim: HAL, the Human Accountability Layer, is where humans hold λ and act as validators, with authority that decay can revoke.
FACT: HAL, the Human Accountability Layer, is where humans hold λ and act as validators, and decay can revoke that authority.
COUNTER: A human with high λ can still be wrong; HAL measures track record, not correctness.
OPINION: Letting decay revoke authority is the strongest part: no one holds power by default.
FICTION: Suppose a validator goes inactive for a year; their λ drifts toward neutral, and the tier they held is gone.
CONTEXT: Named in homage to HAL 9000, 'homage, not aspiration'.

subject: HAL
claim: A HAL seal is the signed record of an authorisation decision and who made it, appended to the ledger.
FACT: A HAL seal is the signed record of an authorisation decision and who made it, appended to the ledger.
COUNTER: Every seal carries separation = none while one key signs everything.
OPINION: The separation field is the honest detail that makes seals meaningful.
FICTION: Suppose a seal shows separation = verified; that's the first proof of independent authorisation.
CONTEXT: hal.py refuses to seal without a verified authoriser score file.

subject: HAL
claim: HAL's two core roles are the Fact Validator, who verifies input data, and the Consequence Authoriser, who seals actions by λ threshold.
FACT: HAL's two core roles are the Fact Validator, who verifies input data, and the Consequence Authoriser, who seals actions by λ threshold.
COUNTER: With one operator, both roles are held by the same person, so the split isn't enforced yet.
OPINION: Separating checking from authorising is right: the person who approves an action shouldn't be the only one who checked its inputs.
FICTION: Suppose the same person validates a fact and authorises acting on it; a single mistake passes both gates.
CONTEXT: Single-operator status is disclosed in docs/hal.md.

subject: Determinism, Replay
claim: A JIG cycle is a pure function of the current state, the active rules and the observation, so the same inputs give the same journal entry byte for byte.
FACT: A JIG cycle is a pure function of current state, active rules and the observation, so the same inputs give a byte-identical journal entry.
COUNTER: Byte-identical output needs canonical serialisation; the stack's own canonicalisation is under-specified for floats and large integers.
OPINION: Determinism is what makes replay meaningful.
FICTION: Suppose a rule reads the clock; the cycle stops being pure, and replay diverges.
CONTEXT: Canonicalisation fix: no fractional numbers, decimal strings, scheme forge-c14n-1.

claim: JIG has a command line and a web app.
FACT: JIG has a command-line interface and a web app.
COUNTER: Two interfaces can drift; nothing here says both expose the same operations.
OPINION: Fine as a fact; it would be stronger naming what each is for.
FICTION: Suppose a rule can be edited in the web app but not the CLI; scripts can't reproduce it.
CONTEXT: Built on a phone in Termux.

subject: Determinism
claim: JIG is a deterministic rule engine: facts, rules, constraints and goals are declared as small signed JSON capsules.
FACT: JIG is a deterministic rule engine in which facts, rules, constraints and goals are declared as small signed JSON capsules.
COUNTER: Small capsules are easy to read individually but hard to reason about together; interactions between rules aren't visible capsule by capsule.
OPINION: Signed rules make every behaviour change attributable.
FICTION: Suppose two rules conflict; determinism needs an explicit resolution order, or the result depends on load order.
CONTEXT: JIG is Canon's substrate.

subject: Replay
claim: JIG records every decision in a hash-chained journal that can be replayed and verified.
FACT: JIG records every decision in a hash-chained journal that can be replayed and verified.
COUNTER: Hash-chaining proves the order wasn't altered, not that the journal wasn't rebuilt from scratch; only a published copy proves that.
OPINION: Replay as audit is the right design.
FICTION: Suppose an old entry is edited; the chain breaks from that row onward.
CONTEXT: Same pattern as ChronoSCRIBE.

subject: Leighton Weight
claim: The Leighton Loop is the stack's pattern of scoring, observing outcomes and updating scores.
FACT: The Leighton Loop is the stack's pattern of scoring entities, observing outcomes and updating the scores.
COUNTER: The 'observe outcomes' step needs signed attestations; without them the loop is score then update with nothing in between.
OPINION: The loop is what keeps λ honest over time.
FICTION: Suppose outcomes are never recorded; λ only decays and never learns.
CONTEXT: Attestations (event.attestation.issued) are the observe arrow.

subject: Leighton Weight
claim: Leighton Weight (λ) is held per entity, ranges from 0.00 to 2.00, and means quarantine below 0.60.
FACT: Leighton Weight (λ) is held per entity, runs from 0.00 to 2.00, and below 0.60 means quarantine.
COUNTER: Capsules don't hold λ; signed or unsigned is binary provenance, a separate thing.
OPINION: Starting new entities at neutral 1.00 avoided the deadlock where newcomers began quarantined.
FICTION: Suppose λ were stored per capsule; a perfect signature would look like perfect trust.
CONTEXT: Scoped per entity and domain; cross-domain aggregation is out of scope.

subject: Provenance
claim: LLLM checks every training doc against its content hash before using it, and names every skipped doc with a reason.
FACT: LLLM checks each training doc against its content hash before using it, and names every skipped doc with a reason.
COUNTER: A hash proves the doc hasn't changed since it was listed, not that it was worth training on.
OPINION: Naming skipped docs is the important part: silent skips are the failure mode James keeps fixing.
FICTION: Suppose a doc is edited after listing; LLLM skips it with a reason instead of training on unlisted text.
CONTEXT: Same 'fail loudly' principle as sign.py's guards.

subject: Provenance
claim: Every word LLLM produces comes from a context that appears in its training docs.
FACT: Every word LLLM produces comes from a context that appears in its training docs.
COUNTER: Traceable words can still combine into a sentence no doc ever said; provenance per word isn't provenance per claim.
OPINION: Word-level traceability is real and rare; the join guard covers the combination risk.
FICTION: Suppose two true sentences are stitched into a false one; every word traces, and the meaning doesn't.
CONTEXT: Links to lllm-refuses-rather-than-invents.

subject: Determinism
claim: The same corpus always gives LLLM a byte-identical model and manifest.
FACT: The same corpus always produces a byte-identical LLLM model and manifest.
COUNTER: Determinism needs the corpus order and tokeniser fixed; a change in file listing order could break it.
OPINION: Byte-identical builds make the model itself verifiable.
FICTION: Suppose the model hash changes with no corpus change; that's proof something nondeterministic crept in.
CONTEXT: Python standard library only.

subject: Python
claim: LLLM trains and runs fully locally, on a phone in Termux or a PC, with no cloud, downloaded weights or GPU, on Python's standard library alone.
FACT: LLLM trains and runs fully locally, on a phone in Termux or a PC, with no cloud, downloaded weights or GPU, on Python's standard library alone.
COUNTER: Fully local limits the corpus to what's on the device and the model to what a phone can train.
OPINION: It's the sovereign path working as intended.
FICTION: Suppose there's no network for a month; LLLM trains and runs unchanged.
CONTEXT: Matches python-for-these-tools.

subject: SQLite
claim: LLLM is a statistical next-word model, not a neural network: it learns context-to-next-word pairs and stores them in SQLite.
FACT: LLLM is a statistical next-word model, not a neural network: it learns context-to-next-word pairs and stores them in SQLite.
COUNTER: Counts learned from text are weights in all but name, so 'no weights' needs care if SymLM's claims lean on LLLM.
OPINION: A model you can query with SQL is unusually inspectable.
FICTION: Suppose someone asks why it chose a word; the answer is a row in a table.
CONTEXT: Being rebuilt as interpreter primitives and capsules.

claim: LLLM uses mixed-order backoff over contexts of 1 to 4 words, so long contexts reproduce the source and short ones let it choose.
FACT: LLLM uses mixed-order backoff over contexts of 1 to 4 words: long contexts reproduce the source, short ones let it choose.
COUNTER: Short-context choices are where invention can happen; that's where the join guard has to work hardest.
OPINION: Making the trade-off explicit, recall versus choice, is good design.
FICTION: Suppose backoff drops to one-word context mid-sentence; output turns fluent but unanchored.
CONTEXT: Links to lllm-refuses-rather-than-invents.

subject: Provenance
claim: LLLM won't train on the canon or lllm repos, because they describe the model and would mean training on its own output.
FACT: LLLM won't train on the canon or lllm repos, because they describe the model and would mean training on its own output.
COUNTER: Other repos may still quote LLLM output; the exclusion catches the obvious loop, not every one.
OPINION: Right rule: a model learning from its own descriptions drifts toward self-description.
FICTION: Suppose a README pastes LLLM output as an example; that text trains the next model unless excluded.
CONTEXT: Same concern as AI-drafted cube faces becoming canon by default.

subject: Provenance
claim: LLLM refuses rather than invents: its join guard stops generation when continuing would stitch unrelated text together.
FACT: LLLM refuses rather than invents: its join guard stops generation when continuing would stitch unrelated text together.
COUNTER: A guard tuned too tight refuses useful output; one tuned too loose lets stitching through.
OPINION: Refusal is the right failure for a system that speaks only on the record.
FICTION: Suppose a sentence needs two sources joined; the guard stops, and the gap is visible instead of papered over.
CONTEXT: Matches Canon's 'refuses what it can't justify'.

claim: LLLM was built for Canon, where a language model is an unreliable witness that may speak only on the record.
FACT: LLLM was built for Canon, where a language model is treated as an unreliable witness that may speak only on the record.
COUNTER: An unreliable witness that's only allowed to repeat the record adds little beyond retrieval; its value is phrasing.
OPINION: 'Unreliable witness' is the clearest framing of how the stack treats any model.
FICTION: Suppose LLLM says something not in the record; Canon treats it as testimony to check, not fact.
CONTEXT: James's own n-gram model.

claim: Replicant's root CHANGELOG.md is a summary. The full Good, Bad and Ugly entries, with Confidence, Risk and Severity ratings, are in python/CHANGELOG.md and rust/CHANGELOG.md.
FACT: Replicant's root CHANGELOG.md is a summary; full Good, Bad and Ugly entries with Confidence, Risk and Severity ratings are in python/CHANGELOG.md and rust/CHANGELOG.md.
COUNTER: Three changelogs can drift; the summary may not match the detail.
OPINION: Recording the Ugly alongside the Good is the plain-words rule applied to history.
FICTION: Suppose a phase appears in the Rust log but not the summary; readers of the root miss it.
CONTEXT: Ratings use 0–10, deliberately not 0.00–2.00, to avoid colliding with λ.

subject: Stigmergy
claim: Replicant's claims decay every tick like pheromones, and OPINION claims are archived once their strength falls to 0.01 or below.
FACT: Replicant's claims decay every tick like pheromones, N(t) = N₀·e^(−kt) per kind, and OPINION claims are archived once strength falls to 0.01 or below.
COUNTER: The README gives the formula but not the 0.01 threshold; that part needs the code.
OPINION: Decaying claims is the core stigmergy idea made into a trust question.
FICTION: Suppose the threshold is 0.1 in code; claims vanish ten times sooner than the cube says.
CONTEXT: Adjudicated claims stay resident rather than being archived.

subject: Adversarial agents, Leighton Weight
claim: Replicant's detection pipeline was verified end to end: fiction claims were adjudicated false, λ penalties logged, and quarantine and expulsion fired.
FACT: James reports Replicant's detection pipeline was verified end to end: false claims adjudicated, λ penalties logged, quarantine and expulsion fired.
COUNTER: The wording 'fiction claims' conflicts with the README, which says Replicant has no FICTION label and catches adversaries by outcome.
OPINION: Reword to 'adversary claims' so it matches the README.
FICTION: Suppose a reader looks for a FICTION label in the code and finds none; the cube looks wrong when the pipeline is fine.
CONTEXT: README: quarantine recovery validated 0.410 → 0.602.

subject: Replicant applications
claim: An emergent signal-vocabulary extension is planned for Replicant, where claim types evolve rather than being fixed.
FACT: James plans an emergent signal-vocabulary extension in which Replicant's claim types evolve rather than being fixed.
COUNTER: Not in the README; and evolving claim types complicates lens classification and adjudication.
OPINION: Strong idea, but it needs its own spec beside agent-diversity-spec.md.
FICTION: Suppose two agents evolve different words for 'food'; adjudication has to know they mean the same thing.
CONTEXT: AI-assisted development to be credited in the README, citing EU AI Act disclosure.

subject: Adversarial agents
claim: Replicant has four adversary types: fiction_planter, hoarder, killer and poisoner.
FACT: James states Replicant has four adversary types: fiction_planter, hoarder, killer and poisoner.
COUNTER: Not named in the README; the README's archetypes are Generalist and Purist, with five proposed.
OPINION: Worth adding to the README or agent-diversity-spec.md.
FICTION: Suppose a hoarder never makes a false claim; outcome-based detection may never catch it.
CONTEXT: Built as AdversaryAgent and AdversaryManager in Python.

subject: Swarm intelligence
claim: Replicant's architecture has four layers: Sensing, Signalling, Action and Reproduction.
FACT: James described a four-layer architecture: Sensing, Signalling, Action and Reproduction.
COUNTER: The README describes a seven-phase tick instead, so the four-layer model may be outdated.
OPINION: Retire it or reconcile it with the tick contract.
FICTION: Suppose a contributor builds to the four layers; their code doesn't fit the seven phases.
CONTEXT: Possibly superseded by the tick contract.

subject: Replicant applications
claim: Replicant's game version makes the player a single agent who has to survive against the odds.
FACT: James decided Replicant's game version puts the player in the swarm as one agent trying to survive against the odds.
COUNTER: Not in the README; status unknown.
OPINION: Playing as one agent makes λ and quarantine felt rather than read.
FICTION: Suppose the player lies once for food; recidivism pricing follows them all game.
CONTEXT: Links to game-making.

claim: Replicant is a hybrid bio-inspired swarm framework built on the Forge Stack.
FACT: The README opens by describing Replicant as a hybrid bio-inspired swarm framework built on the Forge Stack.
COUNTER: 'Framework' implies others can build on it; today it's mainly a research sim with HAL and Merkle signing unfinished.
OPINION: Accurate summary; the two research questions are the interesting part.
FICTION: Suppose someone expects a drop-in swarm library and finds a research sim with open questions.
CONTEXT: Sibling to Keystone Gate in the Forge Stack.

subject: MSL-1.0
claim: Replicant is a Forge Stack consumer with its own capsule namespace and its own consumer ledger anchored to root, under MSL-1.0.
FACT: The README states Replicant holds its own capsule namespace and consumer ledger anchored to root, and inherits MSL-1.0 through every capsule's inherits field.
COUNTER: Anchoring proves where the ledger started, not that it was never rebuilt; only the published copy shows that.
OPINION: Per-consumer ledgers keep Replicant's history its own while traceable.
FICTION: Suppose the ledger is recreated with a fresh anchor; the pushed copy exposes it.
CONTEXT: inherits records governance at signing, not a live pointer.

subject: Leighton Weight
claim: Each Replicant agent's λ is computed from an append-only ledger of decaying events on read, never stored.
FACT: The README says each agent's λ is computed on read from an append-only event ledger; the old cache and verify_cache step are gone.
COUNTER: Computing on read costs more as ledgers grow.
OPINION: Removing the cache removed a whole class of bugs; worth the compute.
FICTION: Suppose a cache disagreed with the ledger; with no cache, there's nothing to disagree.
CONTEXT: Matches the stack rule: λ is never stored.

subject: Leighton Weight
claim: Replicant's λ events decay to a permanent residue, so merit fades and misconduct scars.
FACT: James described λ events decaying to a permanent residue, so merit fades and misconduct scars.
COUNTER: Not in the README, and it conflicts with the stack's neutral-attractor decay.
OPINION: If real, declare it as a consumer override of the stack rule.
FICTION: Suppose the code decays to neutral while the docs say scars; the cube validates a design that isn't running.
CONTEXT: Check the code before validating.

subject: Stigmergy
claim: Each Replicant agent can attest to a claim only once.
FACT: James states each Replicant agent can attest to a claim only once.
COUNTER: Not in the README; without it, one agent could stack attestations to fake consensus.
OPINION: Merge with replicant-claims-close-when-adjudicated; both describe one claim lifecycle.
FICTION: Suppose an agent attests ten times; the claim looks corroborated by one voice.
CONTEXT: Attestation costs energy, which also limits repetition.

subject: Python, Rust
claim: Replicant has parallel Python and Rust implementations of the core sim, and neither is authoritative.
FACT: The README says Python and Rust are parallel implementations, not a prototype and a port, and neither is authoritative.
COUNTER: Equal implementations can drift; feature-parity-spec.md is the only guard.
OPINION: Recording who leads per feature is more honest than naming a reference.
FICTION: Suppose a bug is fixed in Rust only; the parity spec is where that shows, or nowhere.
CONTEXT: Rust leads on archetypes and task priority; Python on analysis tooling.

subject: Replicant benchmarks, Rust
claim: Replicant's earlier "Python wins small" benchmark result was an artefact of timing cargo run's toolchain check.
FACT: James found the earlier 'Python wins small' result came from timing cargo run's build checks, and a rerun with a prebuilt binary showed Rust ahead at every scale.
COUNTER: Not in the README; benchmark_results.json should show the corrected method.
OPINION: The lesson, time the binary not the toolchain, matters more than the ratio.
FICTION: Suppose the old result had shipped; a design decision would have rested on cargo's startup cost.
CONTEXT: Builds moved off the noexec /storage mount.

subject: Leighton Weight
claim: Replicant quarantines agents below λ 0.60 and expels them below λ 0.15, both derived from the ledger.
FACT: The README sets quarantine below λ 0.60 and expulsion below λ 0.15, both derived from the ledger, not latched.
COUNTER: Thresholds are policy choices; their values shape every behaviour result.
OPINION: Deriving status means recovery is possible by design.
FICTION: Suppose expulsion were latched; one bad stretch would remove an agent forever.
CONTEXT: 0.60 matches HAL's quarantine threshold.

subject: Leighton Weight
claim: Quarantined Replicant agents still act, but their attestations carry no weight.
FACT: James states quarantined Replicant agents still act, but their attestations carry no weight.
COUNTER: Not in the README; and the stack's Leighton spec says quarantined attesters keep weak weight rather than zero.
OPINION: Decide which rule Replicant follows and say so.
FICTION: Suppose a quarantined agent correctly flags a poisoned trail; with zero weight, nobody listens.
CONTEXT: Stack rule: acting and observing are separate privileges.

subject: Leighton Weight
claim: Repeat offences in Replicant escalate through a per-agent offences counter, each prior offence adding 100% to the penalty.
FACT: The README says each prior offence adds 100% to the next penalty: one mistake costs −0.08, and three proven lies land at λ≈0.58.
COUNTER: Doubling is steep; a faulty sensor making honest errors could look like lying.
OPINION: Honest agents aren't condemned for one error; repeat liars are.
FICTION: Suppose a damaged agent makes three wrong claims; it's quarantined like a liar.
CONTEXT: Penalties apply at adjudication, never by agents.

subject: Replicant benchmarks, Rust, Python
claim: Rust was faster than Python at every tested scale, averaging 13.1x (range 3.0x to 26.3x) over 16 points.
FACT: James reports Rust ran faster than Python at every tested scale: average 13.1x, range 3.0x to 26.3x, over 16 points.
COUNTER: One machine (a phone under Termux) and one workload; the README quotes no figures.
OPINION: Worth confirming in benchmark_results.json.
FICTION: Suppose the same benchmark on a laptop gives 6x; the ratio was the phone's.
CONTEXT: benchmark.py regenerates benchmark_results.json.

subject: Replicant benchmarks, Rust
claim: Replicant's Rust sim showed a nonlinear timing jump at 100 agents, likely from its linear-scan spatial queries.
FACT: James observed 200 to 500 ticks taking 5x longer instead of 2.5x at 100 agents in Rust.
COUNTER: One observation; the linear-scan spatial query is a hypothesis.
OPINION: Worth a targeted benchmark before optimising.
FICTION: Suppose it's the allocator, not the spatial query; the planned fix misses.
CONTEXT: python/ROADMAP.md flags the linear-scan spatial query.

subject: Rust, WASM
claim: Replicant's Rust sim compiles to WASM and runs in the browser.
FACT: Replicant's Rust sim compiles to WASM and runs in the browser, via rust/wasm.
COUNTER: The built files aren't committed, so the browser build has to be rebuilt to verify.
OPINION: Running in a browser makes the sim easy to share.
FICTION: Suppose a wasm-bindgen update breaks the build; nothing committed shows the last working output.
CONTEXT: analyze_exports.py reads rust/wasm/exports/*.json.

subject: Replicant benchmarks, Python, Rust
claim: The same seed gives different trajectories in Replicant's Python and Rust versions, because they use different PRNGs.
FACT: James found seed 42 gives 9 claims in Python and 35 in Rust, because their PRNGs differ.
COUNTER: Rust's StdRng isn't guaranteed stable across rand versions either.
OPINION: Document it so divergence isn't mistaken for a bug.
FICTION: Suppose a reviewer runs both with seed 42 and reports Rust as broken.
CONTEXT: Within one implementation, the same seed gives the same ledger head hash.

subject: Swarm intelligence, Stigmergy
claim: Replicant borrows mechanisms from seven species: ant pheromone stigmergy, honey bee waggle dance, termite blueprint-less construction, social spider collective capture, paper wasp individual recognition (now replaced by the Leighton Weight Engine), naked mole-rat hypoxia tolerance and aphid parthenogenesis.
FACT: The README maps seven species to mechanisms, from ant stigmergy as a decaying claim field to aphid parthenogenesis as costly replication.
COUNTER: Paper wasp recognition is replaced by the Leighton Weight Engine, so it's inspiration, not an implemented mechanism.
OPINION: The README is right that seven mechanisms alone are a zoo; the couplings are the design.
FICTION: Suppose an entomologist says the mole-rat mapping is oversimplified: the reality check the README asks for.
CONTEXT: The spine couples the mechanisms.

claim: Replicant's tagline is "Born pregnant. Born ready. Born signed."
FACT: The README gives the tagline as 'Born pregnant. Born ready. Born signed.'
COUNTER: Older notes had only two parts, so older docs may disagree.
OPINION: 'Born signed' is the part that separates Replicant from ordinary swarm sims.
FICTION: Suppose a slide quotes the two-part version and misses the provenance point.
CONTEXT: Every agent is born with a signed genome capsule.

claim: Replicant v1.0 has a README.md, a python/ and a rust/ implementation, and a wasm/ browser build.
FACT: The README shows v1.0 as README.md, python/, rust/, wasm/, plus specs and analysis scripts.
COUNTER: A layout goes stale with every restructure.
OPINION: The README's per-folder links keep the root document short.
FICTION: Suppose a folder moves; links in the README break first.
CONTEXT: Status: v1.0, built, tested, running.

subject: WASM
claim: Replicant's WASM folders aren't duplicates: python/wasm/www is the browser UI for the Flask API, rust/wasm builds the Rust sim to WASM, and the root wasm/ holds the browser build, whose built files aren't committed.
FACT: James states the WASM folders aren't duplicates: python/wasm/www is the Flask API's browser UI, rust/wasm builds the Rust sim, and root wasm/ holds the uncommitted browser build.
COUNTER: The README shows only the root wasm/ folder; the layout should be documented in wasm/README.md.
OPINION: Documenting it prevents a well-meaning cleanup from breaking the build.
FICTION: Suppose a contributor deletes two 'duplicate' folders; the browser build breaks.
CONTEXT: Folders exist for the Python vs Rust benchmark.

subject: SCP
claim: SCP, the Semantic Capsule Protocol, produces, validates and consumes sc artefacts, always lowercase, with the extension .sc.json.
FACT: SCP, the Semantic Capsule Protocol, produces, validates and consumes sc artefacts, always lowercase, with the .sc.json extension.
COUNTER: Non-JSON artefacts get a hash pin and a .sig sidecar instead, so not everything SCP handles is an sc.
OPINION: The naming rule keeps code and schemas unambiguous.
FICTION: Suppose a file is named Capsule.json; the rule says it isn't an sc.
CONTEXT: sc v1.2 schema, Ed25519 over canonicalised JSON.

subject: DataCube, HAL
claim: In the SCP substrate each lens is worth 16% of a cube's completeness and human validation 20%, and only a complete cube can be attested.
FACT: In the SCP substrate each lens is worth 16% of a cube's completeness and human validation 20%, and only a complete cube can be attested.
COUNTER: Weights count presence, not quality; five accepted-unread drafts give 80%.
OPINION: Weighting human validation highest is right.
FICTION: Suppose every lens is filled by a model; the cube sits at 80% until a human acts.
CONTEXT: Five lenses × 16% + 20% = 100%.

subject: Leighton Weight
claim: The SCP substrate decays evidence with Forge Theory's formula, N(t) = N₀·e^(−kt).
FACT: The SCP substrate decays evidence with Forge Theory's formula, N(t) = N₀·e^(−kt).
COUNTER: scp-claim resets age_days to 0, so recomputing resets decay, which breaks it in practice.
OPINION: Fix the timestamp before trusting decayed values.
FICTION: Suppose a claim is recomputed daily; it never decays at all.
CONTEXT: The stack's λ decay pulls toward neutral 1.00, not zero.

subject: SCP
claim: The SCP substrate doesn't sign the capsules or cubes it creates itself.
FACT: The SCP substrate doesn't sign the capsules or cubes it creates.
COUNTER: This conflicts with the stack rule that every sc must be signed.
OPINION: Either sign them or record the exception explicitly.
FICTION: Suppose a substrate cube is exported; nothing proves where it came from.
CONTEXT: It does verify signatures on signed imports.

subject: ChronoSCRIBE
claim: The SCP substrate logs every write to an append-only events table, with archiving as the one exception.
FACT: The SCP substrate logs every write to an append-only events table, with archiving as the one exception.
COUNTER: An exception to append-only means it isn't strictly append-only.
OPINION: Log the archive as an event too, and the exception disappears.
FICTION: Suppose a cube is archived; its history leaves the events table with it.
CONTEXT: Not hash-chained or signed yet.

subject: ChronoSCRIBE
claim: The SCP substrate's events aren't hash-chained or signed, so they aren't a ChronoSCRIBE ledger yet.
FACT: The SCP substrate's events aren't hash-chained or signed, so they aren't a ChronoSCRIBE ledger yet.
COUNTER: Unchained events can be edited without trace.
OPINION: Honest naming: calling it a ledger would overclaim.
FICTION: Suppose an event row is edited; nothing detects it.
CONTEXT: Matches datacube-keeps-a-store's naming rule.

subject: DataCube
claim: The SCP substrate's cubes have five lenses, FACT, COUNTER, OPINION, FICTION and CONTEXT, plus human validation, not the six lenses with UNKNOWN that the Forge Stack glossary defines.
FACT: The SCP substrate's cubes have five lenses, FACT, COUNTER, OPINION, FICTION and CONTEXT, plus human validation, not the glossary's six with UNKNOWN.
COUNTER: This contradicts the glossary's six-lens definition.
OPINION: Fits 'DataCube is variable'; the glossary needs updating.
FICTION: Suppose a cube is imported from a six-lens consumer; its UNKNOWN face has nowhere to go.
CONTEXT: Conflicts with datacube-six-lenses.

subject: HAL
claim: The SCP substrate has human validation and attestation, but no HAL tiers or seals yet.
FACT: The SCP substrate has human validation and attestation, but no HAL tiers or seals yet.
COUNTER: Attestation without tiers can't distinguish a trivial cube from a consequential one.
OPINION: Fine for a personal store; tiers matter once others act on cubes.
FICTION: Suppose a shared cube drives an action; there's no tier gate.
CONTEXT: Single-operator, so tiers would record intent only anyway.

subject: DataCube
claim: The SCP substrate doesn't grade cubes as CRYSTALLINE, COHERENT, FORMING or SPARSE yet.
FACT: The SCP substrate doesn't yet grade cubes as CRYSTALLINE, COHERENT, FORMING or SPARSE.
COUNTER: Grades would be easy to compute from the completeness weights already there.
OPINION: Low-cost win if added.
FICTION: Suppose a dashboard sorts cubes by grade; it can't yet.
CONTEXT: Grades defined in datacube-integrity-grades.

claim: The SCP substrate keeps every file under 400 lines and allows no silent exception handlers, and tests enforce both.
FACT: The SCP substrate keeps every file under 400 lines and allows no silent exception handlers, and tests enforce both.
COUNTER: Line limits can push complexity into many small files.
OPINION: Enforcing 'no silent handlers' in tests is the fail-loudly lesson made automatic.
FICTION: Suppose a bare except slips in; the test fails before it ships.
CONTEXT: Same principle as sign.py's guards.

subject: SQLite
claim: The SCP substrate is a personal knowledge store in SQLite, with Keystone Gate as its command line and its page.
FACT: The SCP substrate is a personal knowledge store in SQLite, with Keystone Gate as its command line and its page.
COUNTER: sc.db is committed to the repo, so anything in a cube goes wherever the repo goes.
OPINION: SQLite on a phone is the right fit for a personal store.
FICTION: Suppose a secret is typed into a cube; it's pushed with sc.db.
CONTEXT: Private repo, worked on from Termux.

subject: Leighton Weight
claim: The SCP substrate's standing runs from 0 to 1, fusing a parameter prior with decayed evidence, while the Forge Stack's λ runs from 0.00 to 2.00.
FACT: The SCP substrate's standing runs from 0 to 1, fusing a parameter prior with decayed evidence, while the stack's λ runs from 0.00 to 2.00.
COUNTER: Fusion currently lets a high self-claimed prior dominate weak evidence.
OPINION: Keep standing and λ separately named everywhere.
FICTION: Suppose someone compares a standing of 0.73 with a λ of 0.73; they mean different things.
CONTEXT: Standing belongs to cubes; λ to entities.

subject: SCP
claim: The SCP substrate checks the Ed25519 signature on a signed person or circadian capsule when it imports one, with its own Ed25519 module and did:key encoding.
FACT: The SCP substrate checks the Ed25519 signature on a signed person or circadian capsule when importing it, using its own Ed25519 module and did:key encoding.
COUNTER: The pure-Python Ed25519 isn't constant-time and its RFC vectors only test valid signatures.
OPINION: Fine for verifying your own capsules on your own device.
FICTION: Suppose a malformed signature is imported; Wycheproof vectors would show whether it's rejected.
CONTEXT: See own-ed25519-for-local-signing.
